title: Mental illness as a ground for divorce - evidentiary requirements
p1:
A diagnosis alone does not automatically end a marriage. But many people assume it does.

The real legal question is often not "Is there a mental illness?" but "Can it be proven that the condition affects the marriage in a legally relevant way?"
p2: A surprising fact: courts generally do not grant divorce simply because one spouse has a mental health condition. Evidence usually needs to show factors such as the severity, duration, impact on marital life, and whether the condition makes continuing the relationship unreasonable under the applicable law.
p3:
Medical records, expert opinions, treatment history, and other relevant circumstances may become important pieces of evidence. At the same time, normal stress, temporary difficulties, or unverified claims are usually not enough.

The practical takeaway: in legal disputes involving mental health, facts and evidence matter more than labels.
conclusion: Should divorce laws focus more on the diagnosis itself, or on how a mental health condition affects the reality of married life?
